job.style: a short story with Indian characters in everyday life

response.passage: Rohan and Meera were helping their grandfather fix an old torch in their village home. Rohan noticed the torch had two cells inside. He tried to place them both with their metal caps facing the same direction, but Grandfather gently corrected him, explaining that the positive terminal of one cell must touch the negative terminal of the other for the circuit to work. Meera asked if the electricity gets used up inside the bulb, making the current weaker when it returns to the battery. Grandfather smiled and explained that current is a continuous flow; the bulb simply converts electrical energy into light and heat, but the same amount of current returns to the battery. He then showed them the bulb, pointing out that one wire connects to the base tip and another to the metal casing on the side. He warned them that a circuit is only complete when both these distinct points are connected to the battery. Finally, he tested a piece of dry wood and a plastic scale, noting that while some materials like metals are conductors, many non-metals are insulators, though some special materials can conduct under specific conditions. He reminded them that air is generally an insulator, preventing electricity from jumping across gaps.
response.summary: Grandfather teaches Rohan and Meera how a torch circuit functions by explaining proper cell orientation and the importance of complete connections. He clarifies that current remains constant throughout a circuit and distinguishes between conductors and insulators.
